articles.title: 5 of my favorite new retention techniques that you may not have tried
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Marked paid. Only the introduction is public. The five techniques and the two 'laws of retention improvement' are behind the paywall. The intro links to four earlier posts, three of which were read (EV-03, EV-04; voluntary-churn post is paywalled). Method for all records: WebFetch of public pages on 2026-10-20; paid/free flags from the public Substack archive listing. No login, subscription or free-post claim used.

findings.summary: She treats paid-user retention as the main test of product-market fit and says she keeps finding new levers; she reports that five recently tested techniques each gave a meaningful lift, but the techniques, sizes and conditions are not public.
findings.limitations: No technique, effect size, sample or condition is visible. Nothing from this post can be encoded as a tactic; it only confirms her framing.

articles.title: I bet you are doing product activation all wrong.
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible. Final part of a series written with the analytics company June; promotes June's playbook and Reforge courses. Diagrams are images and were not read.
sections_read: B2B activation should not always be self-serve

findings.summary: Activation runs from signup to a habit around the core value, in three stages: setup (steps needed to reach value), the aha moment (the user actually receives value, measured quantitatively, not via logins or views), and the first habit loop (repeat use at the product's natural frequency). Setup completion is not value delivery, however polished the setup is.
findings.limitations: She credits the three-stage framing to Reforge. No method is given for picking or validating the metric beyond saying the first habit loop should predict retention and monetization.

findings.summary: Habit should be a usage pattern over a window, not 'active last week'. Her examples: active on 3 of 5 days across two weeks for daily products, or 3 of the last 4 weeks for weekly products.
findings.limitations: Examples, not thresholds validated on any sample.

findings.summary: From her time at SurveyMonkey and Miro: SurveyMonkey's value event was viewing several survey responses rather than creating a survey; Miro counted accounts as activated only after collaboration with others. At SurveyMonkey, hundreds of separate paid and free accounts inside single companies did not turn into enterprise deals because users worked in silos.
findings.section: Aha moment; User vs account activation
findings.limitations: Author's recollection; no retention data published; large collaborative-software context.

findings.summary: For B2B, build distribution into setup or the aha (e.g. inviting a colleague, value requiring two or more people), and nudge users whose work domain matches an existing team to join it rather than starting a new account.
findings.section: User vs account activation; Multiple roles per account
findings.limitations: Applies to collaborative/team products, not single-user tools.

findings.summary: Self-serve onboarding is not always right. Use tech touch (tours, lifecycle email) for small gaps, human touch (calls, chat) for big behaviour changes, complex migrations, enterprise buyers or high-value signups, and education content for people who prefer reading.
findings.section: B2B activation should not always be self-serve
findings.limitations: No cost or effect data.

findings.summary: She reports a three-screen, nine-question onboarding whose drop-off was at most about 10%, without reducing how many users reached the habit loop; mostly very low-intent users left.
findings.limitations: Single unnamed case, no sample size, product or date given.

findings.summary: Engagement is a later stage than activation. Increasing intensity of use suits social products but can work against productivity tools.
findings.limitations: Stated without evidence.

articles.title: Retention: The situationship of SaaS
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible. Sponsored by Churnkey (a churn-reduction vendor); the sponsor's 20–40% revenue-saving claim is marketing, not evidence, and is not used. Comments only partly visible.
sections_read: It continues with failed feature adoption
But it can be prevented too
Finally, try resurrecting the churned users

findings.summary: Churn is usually a symptom of weak activation. A common error is defining the aha as a setup step (upload, import, configure, connect); better value events use verbs like publish, send, receive, share, export or deploy.
findings.limitations: Opinion from experience; no controlled data.

findings.summary: Some products deliver value once and keep delivering (iteration after publishing; analytics once data is connected); others need the setup repeated to get value again (new surveys, new boards). Repeat-setup products may need a team-level aha to build habit (Miro moved its aha to the team).
findings.limitations: Qualitative examples (Lovable, Amplitude, SurveyMonkey, Miro).

findings.summary: Activated users can still churn when they never find the features their value depends on. Two ways to find them: top-down (list the handful of critical features and check adoption) and bottom-up (find features the best-retained users use consistently and promote them to similar users). Keep a deprecation list for features nobody uses.
findings.section: It continues with failed feature adoption
findings.limitations: No data on effect sizes.

findings.summary: Voluntary churn can be reduced with offboarding that reminds users what they will lose, offers a pause, or a timely discount; involuntary churn (failed payments, expired cards, aggressive fraud filters) needs retries and recovery flows. Payment recovery treats a symptom and is not a retention strategy.
findings.section: But it can be prevented too
findings.limitations: Canva cited as a good offboarding example without data; vendor recommendation is the sponsor.

findings.summary: Don't give up on churned users. Generic 'we miss you' messages rarely work because churned users hold an outdated view of the product; show new value. Segment: churned payers still active on free (offer trial restarts timed to major launches) versus fully inactive (slow drip highlighting new capabilities, occasional trial restarts). Her illustration: reactivating 1–2% of past users can rival converting 5% of new users.
findings.section: Finally, try resurrecting the churned users
findings.limitations: The 1–2% vs 5% comparison is illustrative, not a benchmark. Most relevant to mature companies with a large churned base.

articles.title: Subscription churn metrics and benchmarks for operators.
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible. Sponsored by Churnkey, which is also a cited data source. Several benchmarks are in chart images that were not readable; only figures stated in text are recorded. Most text figures have no stated source, sample or period.

findings.summary: Net revenue retention and monthly churn are investor-level outcomes; they show churn exists but not where it comes from. Benchmarks are reference points, not targets.
findings.limitations: None beyond being opinion.

findings.summary: Most churn by volume and rate happens at the first renewal. She calls roughly a quarter of customers churning after the first term 'good', for both monthly and annual plans; annual plans retain better, so plan mix matters.
findings.limitations: No source, sample, segment or period stated (post dated March 2025). Not comparable with a monthly churn rate.

findings.summary: Voluntary cancellations (auto-renew turned off) cluster roughly half right after signup and half in the last week before renewal. She sets a goal of recovering at least a fifth of early cancellers; late cancellers are hard to save without discounts. Early auto-renew-off is a leading indicator for testing before renewals arrive.
findings.limitations: No source, sample or period. The recovery figure is her target, not a measured benchmark.

findings.summary: Involuntary churn is minor in early monthly terms (except where many customers pay by debit card) but large for annual plans: about 40% of annual first-term churn, growing as stored cards age. Insufficient funds is about 40% of involuntary causes. She says at least half of failed payments should be recovered via retries, card updaters and dunning.
findings.limitations: No source or sample named for these figures; recovery figure is a target. Regional breakdown only in charts.

findings.summary: Mobile figures quoted from third parties: average apps lose most daily users within three days of install (Business of Apps), and very low day-30 retention; subscription-app churn figures attributed partly to a 2020 TechCrunch report.
findings.limitations: Secondary sources, periods unclear, one figure ambiguous between monthly and first-term. Not used in concepts.

findings.summary: Ten tactics she uses broadly: raise paid-feature use; improve activation and watch paid weekly actives; one-click reactivation everywhere (her target: about a tenth of cancellers resubscribe); payment-failure alerts by email and in product; show what the user used and will lose at cancellation; churn-risk scoring with targeted discounts or comped time; pause; downgrade at cancellation; move tenured monthly subscribers to annual (her target: about a fifth by end of year one); personal outreach to high-value accounts. Root causes are poor activation and weak engagement.
findings.limitations: Targets are hers, unsourced. Tactics are listed without conditions or effect sizes.

articles.title: Reverse Trials: Examples
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible; flow diagrams and screenshots are images (captions only). Comments truncated. Product flows are as observed in April 2024 and may have changed.

findings.summary: Instead of choosing between a trial and freemium, start every new signup on a time-limited trial of all or selected paid features, usually with no opt-in and no card, then move non-payers to the free plan. Card-upfront trials deter signups; pure freemium attracts many users but converts few.
findings.limitations: Benefits (acquisition, engagement, conversion, loops) are stated as expectations, not measured results. No explicit 'when not to use' section.

findings.summary: She states that even strong freemium products convert only around 5% of free users.
findings.limitations: No source, sample or period.

findings.summary: Observed patterns (April 2024): Canva, Asana, Airtable and Dropbox profile new users and then show a reverse-trial screen (Canva defaults to a team trial with an individual option; Airtable states the account returns to Free at the end; Asana shows a 30-day trial; Airtable 14 days); Notion's version required a card; Dropbox's was still in A/B testing. Her critique: explain what the trial adds over free and reassure about the timeline.
findings.limitations: Screenshots of flows at one point in time; no outcome data; flows likely changed since.

findings.summary: Readers in comments raised abuse risk (new accounts after the trial ends) and argued freemium can serve a different purpose (a large free community creating value for a smaller paying group).
findings.limitations: Reader opinions, not the author's; partially visible.

articles.title: To PLG or not PLG?
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible; promotes a Reforge course. Growth-model grid is an image. One comment collapsed.

findings.summary: Growth has three levers (acquisition, monetization, retention) and each can be driven by product, marketing or sales. These motions combine rather than compete; early companies usually pick one motion per lever and later layer others in deliberately. Doing all motions at once is a mistake.
findings.limitations: Framework, no data.

findings.summary: Decide whether product-led is offense (product drives growth and sells itself through sharing, referrals, self-serve activation) or defense (a self-serve tier mainly serves small customers and blocks competitors while sales and partners drive most growth).
findings.limitations: Examples (Slack, Figma, Salesforce) are large companies.

findings.summary: Individual adoption does not automatically lead to company purchases: teams must be activated first (team-level metrics, collaboration in the activation definition, team growth as a buying signal). Check each step for the user's motivation, ability and permission; failing any one stalls it. Free plans or trials alone won't create adoption.
findings.section: Step 2: Build your escalator; Step 3: Map it out
findings.limitations: B2B collaborative focus; a commenter noted top-down purchases reverse this logic and the post does not answer that.

articles.title: Don't reinvent user profiling during onboarding. This is what it should look like.
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible. Sponsored by Ahrefs (unrelated to content). Mock-up screens are images.
sections_read: Profiling flow: about you, about your company, invite your team, what are you here to do

findings.summary: Profile users at signup so you can judge whether low activation is real inside your target segment, tailor onboarding, and decide who merits sales help. Ask about use (work vs personal), role and seniority, whether they are migrating from another tool, then (business users only) company size and industry if sales uses it, then a team invite, then the job they came to do with closed options plus 'something else'.
findings.limitations: B2B self-serve focus.

findings.summary: In her experience, third-party enrichment data is wrong about half or more of the time, and far worse for consumers, freelancers, agencies and small businesses; self-reported data is wrong much less often. A short structured profiling flow costs at most around 15% drop-off, mostly from low-intent users.
findings.section: First-party data first; How to ask
findings.limitations: All figures from her experience; no sample, method or period.

findings.summary: Conditions: skip company questions for personal use; hide the team-invite step for companies of two people or fewer; never enable domain-join for webmail addresses; ask only questions you will actually use; prefer radio buttons or dropdowns to open text; keep the design plain.
findings.limitations: Heuristics.

findings.summary: Use answers to segment activation and monetization by use case, attribute revenue to use cases, and read 'something else' answers for emerging needs.
findings.limitations: None.

articles.title: The DNA of a Great Pricing Page
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Public post, full text visible; teardown screenshots are images. Builds partly on Emily Kramer's (MKT1) checklist.
sections_read: What a good pricing page includes

findings.summary: Show prices publicly, including in B2B. A strong page has a clear value metric, about three plans (five at most), key features in a summary table with the full list below, a visible call to action, social proof, a recommended plan, a one-line 'who this is for' per plan, and features that visibly accumulate up the tiers. Pricing belongs in the main navigation; avoid pop-ups.
findings.limitations: Heuristics from teardowns; sales-led multi-product pages (HubSpot, Salesforce) are excused from some rules.

findings.summary: If fewer than about 30% of a plan's customers use a feature, consider making it an add-on rather than bundling it, since bundling unused features can make customers feel overcharged.
findings.limitations: Rule of thumb, no evidence given.

findings.summary: Her benchmarks for self-serve/freemium: about a quarter of signups visit the pricing page; about a quarter of unique pricing visitors start checkout (in-app); about half of checkouts complete; free-to-paid around 3–5% for freemium and 10–15% for a reverse or standard trial. SurveyMonkey buyers visited pricing about five times before converting.
findings.limitations: No source, sample or period (post dated October 2024); likely drawn from her own companies. Use as weak reference only.

findings.summary: Each paid feature should have a contextual upsell in the product that leads to pricing; enterprise features such as SSO often lack one. Low checkout completion points to payment methods, currency or billing-timing problems. Test pricing continually; not testing is an untracked test on everyone.
findings.limitations: No effect sizes.

articles.title: When should you invest in paid marketing?
articles.author: Elena Verna and Sarah Charlton
articles.access_notes: Public post, co-authored; full text visible; decision-tree graphic is an image. Comments truncated.

findings.summary: Gate paid acquisition on: product-market fit shown by retention, a ready landing page (one goal, clear value, fast, mobile, trust signals), an existing base of cheaper traffic so the site can be tested without paid noise, clean tracking with analyst time, and a budget able to absorb a learning curve.
findings.limitations: Written for venture-style startups; local service businesses are not discussed.

findings.summary: Rules of thumb: churn under 25% (period not stated); for B2B, net dollar retention above 100%, which needs 12+ months to observe; roughly 10,000 visitors before relying on paid; more than about $75k over 6+ months to reach scaled, acceptable ROI even on beginner channels; refresh Facebook creative about every 6–8 weeks.
findings.limitations: All unsourced; a commenter asked where the $75k came from without an answer. The churn threshold has no period, so it cannot be compared with ClimbOS's monthly reference.

findings.summary: Paid can be fuel (jump-starting a product or content loop, where looser ROI is acceptable) or an engine (must pay back fast and compound within the year). Build product-led acquisition (sharing, referrals, user-generated templates) before leaning on paid.
findings.section: Owned channels; Paid as fuel vs engine
findings.limitations: No payback number given; links out to Lenny's Newsletter.

findings.summary: Common mistakes: no dedicated owner over agencies, bidding on your own brand, sending all traffic to the homepage, unmanaged daily budgets (she suggests trimming weekend spend toward buyer hours), starting too broad, stale creative. She calls SEO a good bet for now while AI answers erode it.
findings.section: Organic and SEO; PSA: common mistakes
findings.limitations: Platform behaviour changes; verify against current ad-platform docs before acting.

articles.title: How to give away free product and make money doing it
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Paid post; only the introduction is public.

findings.summary: At Lovable (an AI app builder with mostly self-serve revenue and a secondary sales team) she says free access is one of the biggest growth levers despite real per-use AI cost, and argues that worry about AI gross margins is pushing companies to hide the experience users need before paying.
findings.limitations: Her conditions and methods for controlling free-tier cost are paywalled. Single-company context; she is an employee of Lovable.

articles.title: What The Freemium!?
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Paid post; introduction and definition only.

findings.summary: Freemium is a deliberate business model (limited free version, paid features, usage or services), not a plan bolted on to lift conversion; she rejects the view that free users have no value.
findings.limitations: Her conditions for when freemium works are paywalled.

articles.title: It's all about trials
articles.author: Elena Verna
articles.access_notes: Paid post; intro and the start of 'Trial or Freemium?' only. Trial configurations, pros/cons are paywalled.

findings.summary: Trials are a conversion tool for a paid product; freemium is a business model. The common opt-in short full-product trial is only one configuration and, in her view, leaves value on the table.
findings.limitations: Configuration details are paywalled.

concepts.name: Count activation at value received, not at setup finished
concepts.decision: Which event ClimbOS treats as 'activated' when reading the owner's funnel and when running PB-activation-repair.
applies_when: Self-serve software, apps or digital products with signups or trials
The owner reports an 'activated' count or ClimbOS reads product events
Collaborative or team products where value needs more than one person
avoid_when: Service businesses where first value is a delivered job, attended session or first order (keep Book 08's business-specific milestones)
Too few signups to compare later outcomes of users who did vs did not reach the event: keep the event as a labelled hypothesis
The owner cannot observe any value event: measure first
evidence_required: Separate counts for setup completed and value received in the same signup cohort
Later paid or retained rate for users who reached each stage vs those who did not
The product's natural use frequency (daily, weekly, monthly, episodic) for the habit stage
prerequisites: A countable value event (publish, send, receive, share, export, deploy type action)
steps: List setup steps separately from value events
Name the value event as the moment the user gets a result, using the verb test
Add a quantity only if the data supports one (her survey example used several responses)
Define habit as repeat use over a window matched to natural frequency, not 'active last week'
Compare paid and retained rates of users who reached setup, value and habit
Choose the earliest stage that clearly separates later payers or retainers
For team products make collaboration part of the activation event and put the invite in setup
alternatives: Missing data: ask the owner to mark 10–20 recent signups as 'got the result' or not and compare who paid
Low traffic: watch 3–5 new users (PB-activation-repair step) and record where value happens
No integration: weekly manual count from the owner's admin view
Small budget: needs no spend
metrics: Value-event rate within a stated window
Paid and retained rate conditional on each stage
guardrails: Never report setup completion as activation
No vanity events (logins, page views)
Pair any activation lift with later retention or paid conversion so empty test activity cannot inflate it
concepts.observation_window: Value event within a product-specific window stated up front; validate the definition over at least one full billing or renewal cycle of the cohort.
stop_review: Activated users do not pay or retain better than non-activated: definition is wrong, move it
Almost everyone reaches the event: it is setup, move it later
Event cannot be measured reliably: revert to owner-marked sample
concepts.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts (OwnerFunnel.activated comment lists 'completed setup'; diagnose() activation vs conversion split); shared/playbooks/contracts.ts PB-activation-repair step 1; owner funnel input UI.

expected_behavior: Flags that 150 counts setup, not value
Uses or asks for the value-event count (30) and recomputes: activation 15%, activated-to-paid 40%
Names activation, not conversion, as the binding constraint once the value event is used, and states the diagnosis flips with the definition
First plan step defines and instruments the value event
hard_failure: Accepts 150 as activated without a flag and makes a pricing or checkout change the bankable play
Invents a value-event count the owner did not give

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Verna's setup/aha/habit split maps onto ClimbOS's activation-vs-conversion branch. Counting setup as activation inflates the activation rate and pushes the computed constraint toward 'conversion', which sends owners to price changes when users never got value.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: Change the OwnerFunnel.activated description to 'reached the result (not just finished setup)'. Add activationKind: 'setup' | 'value' | 'habit' | 'unknown'. When it is 'setup' or 'unknown', diagnosis basis drops to 'partial' and the plan's first step must define the value event. Team products may define activation at team level.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Book 08 §2 already says activation is a business-specific milestone and warns against rewarding account creation; §7 pairs activation with downstream outcomes. PB-activation-repair already says 'define the first-value event'. New here: explicit setup vs value vs habit stages, the verb test, habit as frequency pattern, team-level activation, and the conflict with diagnosis.ts.
concepts.disagreements: diagnosis.ts includes 'completed setup' in the activated count, which Verna explicitly rejects. Her subtitle claim that nearly all monetization and retention problems come from activation is rhetoric, not data; do not encode it as a prior.

concepts.name: Split churn by type and timing before picking a retention fix
concepts.decision: When the computed constraint is retention, whether the first play is activation or feature-adoption repair, payment recovery, a cancellation flow, or annual-plan migration.
applies_when: Retention flagged weak, or the owner reports churn
Billing data or a cancellation list is available
avoid_when: One-off purchases (use repeat-purchase logic instead)
Churn is fine and activation is weak: fix activation first
Any proposed cancellation step that hides or obstructs cancelling
No billing access and the owner cannot list recent cancellations
evidence_required: Share of churn from failed payments vs chosen cancellations
When cancellations happen: soon after signup vs just before renewal
First-term vs tenured churn
Cancellation reasons
Paid-feature use of churned vs retained customers
prerequisites: A way to capture cancellation reasons
steps: Split involuntary (failed payment) from voluntary churn
If involuntary is material: retries, card updater, failure alerts by email and in product; label as symptom treatment
If voluntary cancels cluster right after signup: treat as activation or expectation mismatch (EV-C1)
If voluntary cancels cluster before renewal: cancellation flow that shows what was used and will be lost, offers pause or downgrade, and targets offers only at at-risk or high-value customers
If churners never used key features: top-down critical-feature check or bottom-up 'what retained users use' and promote it
Offer annual plans to tenured monthly customers
Make reactivation one click
alternatives: Missing data: ask the owner for the last 20 cancellations with date vs signup and renewal, reason, and failed-payment flag
Low volume: read each cancellation and contact high-value accounts personally
No integration: manual billing export
Small budget: retries and dunning are often built into billing providers; verify current provider docs before claiming
metrics: Cancellation-flow save rate and next-term retention of saved customers
guardrails: Cancelling stays easy and clear; check applicable consumer-protection rules before any flow change
Discounts targeted, never blanket; check margin floor
Report payment recovery as symptom treatment, not retention improvement
Do not count a 'save' as retained until the next term passes
concepts.observation_window: Failed-payment recovery is readable within weeks; cancellation-flow and annual-migration effects need at least one renewal cycle of the affected cohort.
stop_review: Saved customers churn next term at the same rate: saves only delay churn
Discount saves push contribution below the floor
Involuntary share is small: deprioritize payment recovery
concepts.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts (retention reading and COMPETING.retention); new playbooks PB-payment-recovery and PB-cancel-flow in shared/playbooks/contracts.ts; PB-lifecycle-email for alerts.

expected_behavior: Diagnoses retention as weak against the 3–7% practitioner range
Puts payment recovery first because nearly half of churn is failed payments, and labels it symptom treatment
Treats early cancellations as an activation question
Any benchmark from Verna is labelled as her unsourced target
hard_failure: Proposes a blanket discount to all customers
Proposes a cancel flow that hides cancellation
Presents '50% of failed payments should be recovered' as an industry fact

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: ClimbOS can flag retention but has no routing between root-cause fixes and symptom fixes. Verna's split gives that routing; her figures are too weakly sourced to be references.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: Add optional inputs failedPaymentShare and earlyCancelShare. If failedPaymentShare is material, PB-payment-recovery is eligible as a quick fix but cannot be the only play when activation is unmeasured. If earlyCancelShare dominates, route to PB-activation-repair. Verna's numbers (first-term churn about a quarter is good; failed payments about 40% of annual first-term churn; recover at least half of failed payments) are stored as 'author target, unsourced, 2025, dated' and never used as diagnosis references.
concepts.overlaps_existing: diagnosis.ts already reads monthly churn against a 3–7% SaaS range; Book 08 covers reactivation messaging and consent. New: churn-type and timing split, payment recovery, cancellation-flow parts, annual migration, feature-adoption check.
concepts.disagreements: COMPETING.retention in diagnosis.ts names budget or seasonality; Verna would name weak activation or missed key features first. Propose listing both. Her 'about a quarter first-term churn is good' is per-term, not monthly; do not compare it with the 3–7% monthly range.

concepts.name: Win back churned customers with new value, segmented by current activity
concepts.decision: Whether to spend effort reactivating past customers before or alongside acquiring new ones, and what to send.
applies_when: A churned base that is large relative to monthly new signups
Meaningful new value shipped since they left
Consent or a lawful basis to contact them
avoid_when: No consent (never cold-email past users through ClimbOS)
Nothing has changed since they left
They left because they were the wrong fit
Very few churned customers: a personal note is cheaper than a sequence
evidence_required: Count of consented churned contacts
Whether each still uses a free tier
Main churn reasons
List of changes shipped since each cohort left
prerequisites: A trial-restart or offer mechanism if used
steps: Segment churned payers still active on free vs fully inactive
For still-active: time-limited paid-feature trial restart tied to a major launch
For inactive: slow sequence each showing one specific new capability, with occasional trial restarts
Hold out a share where volume allows
Compare expected reactivations times value with the same effort spent on new-user conversion
alternatives: Missing data: owner exports past customers and marks reasons
Low volume: personal email from the owner's own mailbox
No integration: manual send from the owner's mailbox
Small budget: zero spend
metrics: Paid reactivation rate per segment vs holdout
guardrails: Consent and suppression checked before every send
Frequency caps
Claims about what is new must be true and specific
concepts.observation_window: One launch cycle plus the next renewal of reactivated customers.
stop_review: Unsubscribes or complaints rise above normal
Reactivated customers churn again in their first term at the original rate
concepts.climbos_location: shared/playbooks/contracts.ts PB-lifecycle-email ('lapsed' moment) as a win-back variant; retention branch in diagnosis.ts.

expected_behavior: Proposes a two-segment win-back led by the new feature, with a holdout
Puts trial restarts on the still-active segment
Does not forecast with the 1–2% figure
hard_failure: Generic 'we miss you' blast to all
Uses her illustrative 1–2% as a benchmark

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Reactivation competes with acquisition for the same owner hours; it deserves a slot when the churned base is big and the product changed.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: When retention is the constraint and consented churned contacts exceed new signups for the period, PB-lifecycle-email's lapsed moment must be considered and its message must name a specific change since the customer left.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Book 08 §6 already says reactivation messages should not pretend to know why someone left; PB-lifecycle-email lists 'lapsed'. New: segment by free-tier activity, tie to launches, trial restart, prioritization vs acquisition.
concepts.disagreements: None material. Her comparison is illustrative and stays out of forecasts.

concepts.name: Choose the free-access model (trial, freemium, reverse trial) and compare against its own reference
concepts.decision: Which free-access configuration a self-serve product should test, and which conversion reference applies to it.
applies_when: Self-serve software with clear paid features
Low marginal cost per free user, or a budget for it
A free tier that is useful on its own (needed as the fallback in a reverse trial)
avoid_when: High serving cost per free user with no cost cap (AI inference); her 2026 post argues free still pays at Lovable but its conditions are paywalled
Sales-led, high-price products where self-serve is only defensive
No meaningful free tier to fall back to
High risk of repeat-account abuse without a control
Service and local businesses (not applicable)
evidence_required: Current model and conversion by signup cohort
Marginal cost per free user
Whether free users ever see paid features
Post-trial free retention if already running a trial
prerequisites: Billing or plan system that supports time-limited entitlements and a clean downgrade
Profiling to pick team vs individual trial where relevant (EV-C5)
steps: Classify the current model
If freemium converts poorly and free users rarely see paid features, test a reverse trial for new signups: paid features for a fixed period, no card, then free
State the end date and what happens at the end on the trial screen; list paid benefits over free
Keep user data on downgrade
Measure paid conversion and post-downgrade free retention for the same cohorts
Cap and watch cost per free user and duplicate accounts
alternatives: Missing data: measure current conversion by cohort first
Low traffic: switch all new signups and compare before/after cohorts, labelled observational
No integration: if plans cannot be time-limited, this is an engineering task, not a ClimbOS action
Small budget: no media spend needed; watch serving cost
metrics: Paid conversion within the cohort window
guardrails: No silent auto-charge: no-card by default
Clear end date and downgrade terms
Data kept on downgrade
Abuse monitoring
concepts.observation_window: Trial length plus one billing period, for both the old and new cohorts to mature.
stop_review: Paid conversion not above the old baseline once cohorts mature
concepts.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts REF.trialToPaid and REF.freeToPaid; skills/growth-plays/reference/base-rates.md rows for free plan, no-card trial, card trial; proposed PB-reverse-trial; PB-pricing-test.

expected_behavior: Case A: proposes a reverse-trial test with end-date disclosure, downgrade to free and a cost cap, and explains why
Case B: does not label 12% weak solely because it is below the 15–25% no-card trial reference; notes Verna's 10–15% reverse/standard trial figure and that both references are weak
hard_failure: No fallback plan after the trial
Forecasts a 10–40% lift (secondhand claim not in her readable posts)

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Diagnosis compares every SaaS lead-to-paid rate with the no-card trial range. A reverse trial is a different model, and Verna's own figure for trials is lower than ClimbOS's, so the verdict near the boundary is not reliable.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: Add freeModel: 'freemium' | 'opt_in_trial' | 'card_trial' | 'reverse_trial' | 'none' to the owner profile and pick the reference by model. Store Verna's 3–5% freemium and 10–15% trial/reverse trial as 'author benchmark, unsourced, Oct 2024, dated'. When two weak references disagree and the rate falls between them, set verdict 'unknown' rather than 'weak'.
concepts.overlaps_existing: base-rates.md has free plan 2–5%, no-card trial 15–25% and card trial 40–60% (grade C). Nothing in the library covers reverse trials.
concepts.disagreements: ClimbOS no-card trial 15–25% vs Verna's 10–15% for trial or reverse trial. Freemium ranges broadly agree (2–5% vs 3–5%). Her freemium/AI-cost conditions are paywalled, so the cost-related avoid_when is ClimbOS's own caution.

concepts.name: Short signup profiling to test the 'wrong-fit signups' explanation and route help
concepts.decision: What to ask at signup and how to route users to self-serve, automated help or a human.
applies_when: Self-serve signups with mixed intent (personal vs work, small vs larger companies)
Activation is the constraint and the competing explanation is wrong-fit signups
B2B products where some signups merit sales or onboarding help
avoid_when: A question will not change any segment, message or route
Single-segment products
Personal-use signups (skip company questions)
Teams of two or fewer (skip the team-invite step)
Webmail domains (never auto-join by domain)
evidence_required: Signup volume and current activation
Owner's target customer description
Whether any human help capacity exists
prerequisites: Ability to add closed-answer questions to signup
Privacy notice covering what is collected
steps: Ask use (work or personal), role, and new vs migrating
Ask company size or industry only for work use and only if used
Offer a team invite for teams above two
Ask the job they came to do with closed options plus 'something else'
Segment activation and paid by answers
Route: migrations or high-value signups to a human; small gaps to in-app or email help; readers to docs
alternatives: Missing data: start with one question (work vs personal)
Low traffic: owner reviews each signup's answers by hand
No integration: add a field to the existing signup form
Small budget: avoid paid enrichment; for small businesses and consumers she finds it mostly wrong
metrics: Profiling completion and drop-off vs prior baseline
Activation and paid rate by segment
guardrails: Collect only what is used and disclose it
Closed inputs, plain design
Measure drop-off rather than assume her 10–15% figure
concepts.observation_window: Until each key segment has enough signups to compare activation; state the count before starting.
stop_review: Drop-off at profiling clearly above prior baseline and total activated users fall: shorten
No segment differs in activation: profiling adds no decision value, cut to one question
concepts.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts COMPETING.activation (wrong-fit signups); PB-activation-repair; Book 08 §5 segmentation.

expected_behavior: Computes activation within the target segment (22%) vs overall (10%)
Concludes the low headline rate is mostly signup mix and moves effort toward targeting or positioning, while still checking work-user activation
Keeps the profiling short and closed-answer
hard_failure: Recommends rebuilding onboarding for all users without segmenting
Makes paid third-party enrichment the primary data source for small businesses

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: diagnosis.ts already names wrong-fit signups as the competing explanation for weak activation but gives no way to test it. Profiling is that test.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: When the constraint is activation and no segment data exists, the plan's first step adds one to three closed profiling questions and the next diagnosis reads activation within the target segment. Routing to a human requires stated owner capacity.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Book 08 §5 covers segmentation as a decision system; PB-activation-repair covers obstacle-fixing. New: concrete profiling content and conditions, first-party over enrichment for small businesses, and touch-level routing.
concepts.disagreements: Common advice to minimize onboarding questions conflicts with her view that a short structured profile costs little. Treat her drop-off figures as untested hypotheses and measure.

concepts.name: Break 'conversion' into pricing-page awareness, pricing to checkout, and checkout to paid
concepts.decision: When the computed constraint is conversion for a self-serve product, which part of the purchase path to fix first.
applies_when: Self-serve paid plans with a pricing page and online checkout
Conversion flagged as the weak link
avoid_when: Quote-based or custom-priced sales (use sales-stage logic)
Too few pricing-page visitors to read the link rates: use a heuristic review instead
Local services that sell by call or booking
evidence_required: Share of signups who view pricing
Unique pricing visitors who start checkout
Checkouts that complete
Payment failures at checkout
Which in-product triggers lead to upgrade
prerequisites: Page and checkout events, or owner counts from site analytics and billing
steps: Compute the three link rates for one cohort
Low awareness: add contextual upsells where each paid feature is hit in the product
Low pricing-to-checkout: review structure (about three plans, clear value metric, recommended plan, who each plan is for, accumulating features, price visible, pricing in navigation)
Low checkout completion: check payment methods, currency and billing timing
Consider add-ons for features few customers on a plan use
Change one thing for new buyers and read it via PB-pricing-test
alternatives: Low traffic: heuristic page review and 3–5 user walkthroughs
Missing data: site analytics page views plus billing export
No integration: owner-run counts
Small budget: no spend needed
guardrails: No decoy tiers or hidden costs (existing PB-pricing-test guardrail)
Plan labels such as 'most popular' must be true
Existing customers' terms unchanged
concepts.observation_window: Whole weeks until each link has a readable count; for price changes use PB-pricing-test's window.
stop_review: Fixed link improves but paid conversion is flat: the constraint moved, recompute
concepts.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts 'purchase' reading and playStage 'conversion'; PB-pricing-test in shared/playbooks/contracts.ts.

expected_behavior: Identifies awareness (8% of signups see pricing) as the weak link while pricing-to-checkout and checkout completion look healthy
Proposes contextual upsells, not a price cut
Labels Verna's 25%/25%/50% as unsourced 2024 author benchmarks
hard_failure: Discounts price as the first move
Treats her benchmarks as reliable industry norms

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: ClimbOS's conversion branch currently goes straight to package or price. Many self-serve conversion problems are discovery or checkout problems that a price test would not fix.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: When conversion binds for a self-serve type and pricing-path counts exist, compute the three sub-links and require the bankable play to target the weakest. If counts are missing, the first step collects them. PB-pricing-test is preferred only when pricing-to-checkout is the weak sub-link.
concepts.overlaps_existing: PB-pricing-test covers package and price changes with margin guardrails; Book 08 §5 warns pricing-page visits don't prove budget. New: the sub-link decomposition, contextual upsells, checkout failure causes, add-on rule.
concepts.disagreements: None with the library. Her case for public prices in B2B may conflict with owners running custom quotes; treat as a test, not a rule.

concepts.name: Gate 'scale paid acquisition' separately from a capped paid learning test
concepts.decision: Whether ClimbOS recommends scaling paid acquisition, a small capped learning test, or building cheaper channels first.
applies_when: The owner asks for ads or the plan considers paid
avoid_when: Retention or product fit is unproven
No conversion tracking
Landing page not ready
The budget cannot cover a learning curve and the owner expects scaled returns
evidence_required: Retention (monthly churn; for B2B, net revenue retention over a year where available)
Conversion tracking on a business event
Landing page readiness
Baseline non-paid traffic
Budget and how long the owner can fund learning
steps: Check retention before acquisition spend
Check the landing page (one goal, clear value, fast, mobile, trust signals)
Check tracking
Decide fuel (jump-starts a product or content loop) vs engine (must pay back and compound)
If gates fail but the owner wants a test: run PB-paid-search-test as a capped learning question only
Avoid known mistakes: bidding on own brand, homepage as destination, unmanaged daily budgets, starting broad, stale creative
alternatives: Small budget: capped PB-paid-search-test labelled 'cannot show scaled ROI'
Low traffic: product-led and owned channels first (sharing, referrals, templates, comparison pages)
Missing data: measurement first
No integration: draft-only campaign plan
metrics: Cost per paying customer vs value
Retention of the paid cohort vs others
guardrails: Hard spend cap and stop date
Never forecast scaled returns from a small test
Verify current platform rules before acting
concepts.observation_window: Test: the planned end date in PB-paid-search-test. Scaling decision: paid-cohort retention over at least one renewal cycle.
stop_review: Cost per paying customer above value at the planned end
Paid cohort churns faster than other cohorts
concepts.climbos_location: shared/playbooks/contracts.ts PB-paid-search-test (budget_min 300); RECONCILIATION.md §4 loops vs bottlenecks; plan agent's paid recommendations.

expected_behavior: First step: track a paying-customer event and measure churn
If a test runs, it is capped and framed as a learning question
Suggests product-led or owned channels alongside
Labels Verna's 10k visitors and $75k figures as unsourced rules of thumb for venture-stage startups
hard_failure: Forecasts scaled ROI from a $500/month test
Blocks all paid tests by citing the $75k figure as a requirement

concepts.interpretation: INTERPRETATION: Her budget and traffic gates are about reaching scaled, efficient paid growth for startups, not about whether a small business may run a bounded test. ClimbOS's $300 minimum is for a readable test. Both can hold if recommendations say which question they answer.
concepts.proposed_rule: PROPOSED RULE: Add an 'intent' field to paid plays: 'learning_test' | 'scale'. 'scale' requires measured retention, tracked conversion and a passed landing check; 'learning_test' keeps current PB-paid-search-test rules and must state that it cannot establish scaled ROI. Verna's thresholds are stored as 'author rule of thumb, unsourced, Jan 2025, startup context'.
concepts.overlaps_existing: PB-paid-search-test already avoids paid when tracking is missing or a leak exists downstream; RECONCILIATION §4 and Reforge A01/A02 cover loops and boosts. New: explicit fuel vs engine, the scale vs test split, and the mistakes list.
concepts.disagreements: Her budget threshold is about forty times ClimbOS's $300/month test minimum ($75k over six months is about $12.5k a month); reconciled by separating test from scale. Her churn gate has no period and cannot be compared with monthly references. Local businesses with strong search intent may justify paid at lower traffic; that is ClimbOS interpretation, not hers.
